subsubtopic: AIR CANADA URGED TO INCLUDE NEWFOUNDLAND AND SASKATCHEWAN IN PROMOTION OF TOURISM- MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The latest promotional program of Air Canada, called "Share Canada", under Maritime Explorer Tours, Atlantic Freedom, Canaplan, Canadapass, Canada Fly Drive, Summertime Spectaculars, Motorhome Camping Vacations, and others, extols the virtues of holidaying in every province but Newfoundland and Saskatchewan. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House directs the Minister of Transport to correct this discriminatory oversight by Air Canada and that immediate appointments be made to the board of directors to include those provinces to ensure recognition of Newfoundland and Saskatchewan as important sectors of our nation in all phases of economic activity and to allow all Canadians to enjoy the beauty and attraction of those provinces, as well as the others.

subtopic: COMMONWEALTH DAY-PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HIGH COMMISSIONERS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMMONWEALTH DAY-PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HIGH COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. members will join with me, before beginning question period, in calling attention to the significance of this day, Commonwealth Day. I have had the good fortune and honour, on behalf of parliament, of inviting some members of the House of Commons to a reception-luncheon to receive the High Commissioners of Commonwealth countries.
Perhaps we might pause for a moment before the question period to call attention to their presence in the gallery and to recognize the significance and value of our connection with the Commonwealth of Countries which all of us support and regard as an association of countries long past the historical sense and now having reached a voluntary association of peace-loving countries who espouse the best of all ideals between the developed and developing nations. It is an association between those who endeavour to reach out and help each other, which in that connection has some basis in history but, more importantly, in modern times it is a voluntary arrangement of friendship and association of the best ideas espoused by all of us in public life.
I hope that all members of the House will join me in signalling the presence of these Commonwealth High Commissioners, to call once more into attention and prominence the

March 13, 1978

importance of our birthright and our connection with the Commonwealth of Nations.

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. We have now had an opportunity to review the preliminary prospectus filed by Canada with the SEC in Washington, covering the issue of $750 million in foreign bonds to be sold in that country, and the prospectus indicates:
-the bonds will be free of all present and future taxes imposed by Canada or any province thereof or by any taxing authority thereof or therein-
In view of this, would the Minister of Finance indicate why it was felt advisable-indeed, even necessary-to propose such a luscious deal to those who might be buying these bonds?

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at this moment I do not have any comment. I will look into the matter. I do not have the text that has been used by the hon. member, and 1 would like to review it before I answer.

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I would have assumed that the Minister of Finance would have reviewed this prospectus thoroughly, and I am rather surprised he is using the "out" that he does not know the wording. Let me ask a further question. The prospectus also states that the underwriting agreement which presumably will be signed by the government and various underwriters will be conditional upon there being-
-no material adverse change or any development involving a prospective material adverse change in the financial, economic or political conditions of Canada from those set forth in the registration statement.
My question to the minister is whether officials in the Department of Finance have received an unqualified legal opinion that the deficit, which is estimated to be $14 billion in the current year, is not a material change which would break this contract, bearing in mind that such a deficit might be 50 per cent larger than the deficit disclosed in this prospectus.

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION
speechtext: I am glad that the market does not take the hon. member too seriously, because he is always throwing about some big figures and starting rumours that have no basis in reality. That is why I know those people do not pay too much attention to the hon. member.

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION

subsubtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PROSPECTUS FILED WITH U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION

subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the announcement that Northwest Energy Corporation, a partner of Foothills in the construction of the northern pipeline, has just signed contracts for Alberta gas which will increase Canadian exports to the United States by 37 per cent. In view of the fact that Canada's long-term prospects for gas are not reassuring, what guidelines has the government given the National Energy Board regarding the amount of gas reserves which must be held to meet future Canadian needs, and what percentage will be declared surplus to our national requirements and allowed to be exported?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is somewhat premature. The application has yet to be presented to the National Energy Board for a decision and, as I am sure the hon. member is also aware, it will depend a good deal on the Alberta government and the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board assessment of the reserves position in that province as to whether gas would be available for export on a swap basis.
I have noted the interest with respect to the application to move, as the hon. member has indicated, close to a billion cubic feet of gas to the United States. I understand that that particular proposal is on the basis of a swap arrangement whereby Canadians would have a call on future gas reserves from Alaska, and to that extent this proposal is consistent with the position the government has already made public.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has said, this could mean the export of a billion cubic feet of gas per day to the United States under some type of swap arrangement. I therefore ask the minister if what we have been told, that the Alcan gas pipeline was to take Arctic gas to the United States, is now being put in second place, and the primary purpose of this pipeline now will be to take cheap Alberta gas to the United States in order to give Canadians the "privilege" of buying expensive Arctic gas in the future.
I ask the minister if that is the understanding which has been reached between the government, Foothills and Northwest Energy Corporation. Also, will he tell the House the terms upon which such as a swap arrangement will be made?
Oral Questions
Are we to buy dear gas and sell cheap gas: is that the swap arrangement the government has in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the first point, quite clearly the government's interest in the Foothills (Yukon) pipeline in energy terms is to gain access to Canadian supplies at low cost. The option for Canada is that we will be able to move Canadian supplies to Canadian customers for less money than the United States will be able to move their gas to United States' customers. As to the details of the swap arrangement, I have to say that I do not believe they have got them worked out. The kind of guarantees the hon. member is seeking are very much present in our minds as well.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext:
A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the final arrangement would have to be approved by the cabinet, and in view of the fact that originally in the National Energy Board there was a stipulation that the government had to hold 21 years of gas in reserve, and that provision was taken out, I ask the minister if he will tell the House, in all fairness, the quantity of gas the National Energy Board will be asked to keep in Canada before declaring that any other gas is surplus to national requirements.
Surely that ought to be known. It is not a matter for the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board or any other agency. The Canadian government will have to approve any export of gas recommended by the National Energy Board, and this parliament has a right to know how much gas is to be held for the future requirements of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES TO NEB ON GAS RESERVES FOR CANADIAN NEEDS
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, the National Energy Board is charged by parliament with this responsibility. We will be looking to the National Energy Board for advice on whether the gas that is proposed might be moved on some kind of accelerated or swap basis will in any way change the situation as far as that gas being surplus to Canadian needs is concerned. If it is on a swap basis-which I understand it is intended that gas would be-I cannot see that that would change in any way the whole question of surplus, or not surplus, to Canadian needs.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RRAP WILL BE INSTITUTED THROUGHOUT CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.

March 13, 1978
OraI Questions
Some time ago, the minister implied that RRAP would be extended throughout Canada without consideration for obstacles that could occur at provincial level. Could he say now to the House if he is going to institute that program? Will he also announce it soon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RRAP WILL BE INSTITUTED THROUGHOUT CANADA
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Negotiations are currently going on with each province to extend designations under RRAP, more likely in all rural Canada and in a greater number of Canadian cities. RRAP already applies to almost all rural Canadian territory and, of course, that means we will have to increase considerably the funds available for such a program. That is what we will do and at the same time we will urge those who are responsible for the implementation of that program to serve first families which have lower incomes, second those who live in the oldest houses of the country, and third, they will be asked to give priority to people inhabiting regions already designated under this program.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RRAP WILL BE INSTITUTED THROUGHOUT CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does that mean that it will no longer be necessary for a rural area to get the approval of the provincial government, and here I am thinking specially of the province of Quebec, because now the area must be designated by the provincial government? Will that provision disappear, and will that cover the whole area, as the minister just said, without having to get provincial authorization to determine an area?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RRAP WILL BE INSTITUTED THROUGHOUT CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the approval of the provincial authorities will always be needed for designating purposes. Still, in the case which surely interests the hon. member, I can say that our negotiations with the provincial authorities have enabled us to extend designations widely to all rural areas of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, as this matter is extremely important, and in view of the numerous requests we get in this regard, will the funds be increased considerably to allow approval of a rather large number of requests so that more people can benefit from this program I consider absolutely marvellous? An hon. member of the opposition does not often say things like that!

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, naturally we will increase considerably the funds allotted to each province of Canada for the application of this program. But as we suspect that those funds will not be sufficient to meet the demand, we are therefore recommending that applications from low-income earners be dealt with first, and secondly those of people who live in the oldest houses in the country, and thirdly, those from areas that were first designated. Nothwithstanding those three basic recommendations, obviously we will have to increase, probably double, or even triple, the funds allotted to each province: we hope to be in a position to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. The Prime Minister, in a press conference over the weekend, confirmed that the Economic Council of Canada will be acting as a monitoring agency in the post-control strategy of the government after the Anti-Inflation Board finishes its mandate. He also confirmed that the agency will not have any authority to inquire into or act upon specific wage and price increases.
I would like to ask the minister, in light of the paradox that this proposes for an agency which will be acting post facto-in other words, before it can report to the government, it will have to identify wage and price increases in a specific sector or company-what agency does the government intend to use to act on such wage or price increases that have been so identified by the ECC, in view of the fact there will be no legislative authority after the AIB mandate finishes on April 15?

subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have said that after April 14 we are going back to the market-place and we do not intend to have legislation that will give power to the government to roll back either wages or price increases.

subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the minister explain to the House why the Economic Council of Canada has not been given the legislative authority to examine or investigate areas of potential wage and price increases that would go beyond the guidelines? In other words, the only role they will have will be to analyse statistics which are already in the public domain, the statistics from Statistics Canada, a role which the cabinet itself could carry out. I ask the minister why the Economic Council has not been given the legislative authority that the Food and Prices Review Board had, to inquire into and open up the books in areas where the guidelines have been exceeded.

subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have decided that after April 14 we will not have controls. The hon. member is trying to find a way to keep controls. Members of the opposition should make up their minds. They have been asking us to remove controls for the past two years.

subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext:
What the minister is telling the House and the country is that the government, in fact, has no post-control strategy. That is the situation facing us today. I ask the minister to tell the House what authority or what method of operation the government has in mind once a problem area has been identified by the ECC as going beyond the guidelines.

March 13, 1978

How would the government act, faced with such a report by the ECC?

subsubtopic: MONITORING AGENCY FOR POST-CONTROLS PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are not planning to have a roll-back provision in any legislation. We are hoping people will understand the consequences of being under controls. We are removing controls. The Economic Council of Canada will look at price and wage developments and make comments. If it sees a difficult situation, perhaps we can have a specific inquiry. We are going to back in the market-place. We hope the public will react as we have some indication they will; they are very responsible.

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. As Your Honour mentioned, today is the anniversary of the Commonwealth. Today is also the sixty-fifth anniversary of the first woman obtaining a pilot's licence in Canada. Eileen Vollick received her pilot's licence on this date in 1913, flying a Curtis Jenny biplane. In view of the fact that women have been licensed as pilots for the past 65 years in Canada, can the minister explain why it is still the policy of the Department of National Defence not to have any women pilots in National Defence, in view of their obvious acceptance by the Ministry of Transport for over 50 years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a subject that is constantly under review.

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: The difficulty really resolves itself in relation to women serving in combat, which is something, quite frankly, we have not come to grips with: no western nation really has. Our pilots are versatile and must perform many roles. It does create a problem-one which we are examining-in so far as women serving in combat is concerned. We have not yet made a decision as to what is an appropriate role, after the experience of other nations which have tried that and found it quite demoralizing, not because women cannot stand it but because men in combat with them emotionally are not able to accept it.

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this must establish a new record of constant review, having gone on for 65 years. Combat is only one of the areas where women pilots in other countries have performed with remarkable effectiveness and skill. What steps is the department actually taking to resolve this very serious anomaly in its structures? In view of the constant review that has been going on for over half a century,
Oral Questions
can the minister indicate when the review will be brought to a satisfactory conclusion?

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the constant review has resulted in concrete results in the armed forces, where women are increasingly effective in the roles in which they are serving. Just this past week I announced the addition of women to the advisory council to the Canadian military colleges. This matter has received active consideration. I have spent a great deal of time with my officials and senior commanders in all areas, and women are increasing their role in the Canadian armed forces. We have not made the decision to put them in roles where they either have to be in combat or rotate with those in combat, due to the manning ratios we have to live with.

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS
speechtext: In view of the concern expressed by a number of young women who in recent years have applied for admission to the armed forces in a variety of skills and tasks, is the minister prepared to table in this House within the next few weeks a statement as to the number of trades and skills that are still prohibited from the interests of women? Will he also give some indication, in terms of the career and officer training program with respect to military colleges, in view of the comment he just made, of how soon there may be a satisfactory resolution of the very real discrimination that exists with respect to complete training facilities for women in Canada's armed forces?

subsubtopic: REASON DEPARTMENT DOES NOT EMPLOY WOMEN PILOTS

subsubtopic: RESEARCH CENTRE AT WINNIPEG, MAN.-INTENTIONS RESPECTING CONSTRUCTION

subtopic: EXPENSES IN CONNECTION WITH SEARCH FOR SOVIET COSMOS SATELLITE
EXPENSES IN CONNECTION WITH SEARCH FOR SOVIET COSMOS SATELLITE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a two-part question for the Minister of National Defence with regard to the Cosmos satellite. First, has the minister read outer space treaties Nos. 6 and 7, and is he satisfied that we have complied with both treaties? Second, the minister assured the House on January 30 that he was keeping a careful record of expenses. Can he inform the House what the expenses of the search have been so far?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: EXPENSES IN CONNECTION WITH SEARCH FOR SOVIET COSMOS SATELLITE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not read those treaties recently. The first time I read them, I thought it was quite enough. My advice is that we are complying with them. With regard to the second part of the question, we are keeping track of the expenses. The total recovery cost, from the point of view of the Department of National Defence, is in excess of $4.7 million at this time. That does not include other departments of the federal government.

subtopic: EXPENSES IN CONNECTION WITH SEARCH FOR SOVIET COSMOS SATELLITE
speechtext: I asked the minister if he had read the treaties, because they clearly differentiate between the cost of the search and the expenses and costs of damages. It seems the government has never been able to learn this clear differentiation. We seem to have convinced the Russians that they are to pay for the damages, which are nil, and they have convinced us we are to pay for the expenses, which will be nearly $5 million. This kind of a deal we can do without. Does the minister plan to point out to his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that the expenses are no part of the damages and it says so in the treaty?

subtopic: EXPENSES IN CONNECTION WITH SEARCH FOR SOVIET COSMOS SATELLITE
speechtext:

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-4, to amend the Aeronautics Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
That Bill C-4, on Act to amend the Aeronautics Act, be amended in Clause 2 by adding immediately after line 9 at page 2 the following:
"(2) (a) All regulations made pursuant to this section are subject to
negative resolution of the House of Commons.
(4) Notwithstanding paragraph (a), where a motion for the consideration of the House of Commons, signed by not less that twenty Members of the House, is filed with the Speaker to the effect that regulations made pursuant to this section be referred to a Standing Committee of the House so that witnesses may be heard and a report may be made to the House, the House of Commons shall, within the first fifteen days next after the motion is filed that the House is sitting, in accordance with the rules of the House, take up and consider the motion, and if the motion, with or without amendments, is approved by the House such regulations shall be so referred to the Committee.
(c) Where regulations are referred to a Committee pursuant to paragraph (b) and the Committee makes a report thereon, such report shall be tabled in the House of Commons and following a debate of no longer than four hours, there shall immediately be a vote on the motion to approve the regulations with or without amendments."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am compelled to move this amendment at this time because Bill C-4, numbered Bill C-40 in the last session of this parliament, is a classic illustration of how a paternalistic government, tainted with arrogance, will use a sledgehammer approach to correct a technical deficiency in a piece of legislation and, in the process, impose some very repressive terms and conditions upon innocent victims who are very seriously implicated and affected by such changes. This piece of legislation is clearly an example of an overpowering

government flexing its bureaucratic muscle without having any regard for the people it will affect.
Just to review the history of this bill briefly, it was introduced into the House of Commons for second reading last June. At that time the minister stated that the bill was of a highly technical nature and that it was needed to deal more effectively with the safety and licensing administration as it relates to aircraft, operators of aircraft, and facilities which are licensed pursuant to the terms and conditions which are spelled out by the Ministry of Transport.
The minister went on to say that the bill was needed for the purpose of improving the method of collection of fees for services rendered by the Ministry of Transport, that the bill would provide for the imposition of interest charges on past due accounts arising therefrom, and also would provide a mechanism for the provision of a security bond, a contract or a letter of credit reference for anyone using the services and facilities of the Ministry of Transport. Quite frankly, some clauses of the bill are aimed at tightening up the collection process. Further, the bill provides for mechanisms with respect to dealing with zoning and development of land in and around airport facilities.
Because this bill is of a rather highly technical nature, ostensibly termed as a housekeeping measure, the minister sought concurrence from the House to proceed through all stages of this legislation, which would have meant that it would have passed second reading, committee stage, and third reading all within the walls of the chamber of the House of Commons. This party denied that concurrence and pointed out that the bill should be referred to the committee and witnesses called in order that there be a better understanding and thorough explanation of the legislation.
It became obvious very quickly at committee that the bill contained some very undesirable features relating to general aviation, particularly in the small aircraft sector. It soon became apparent to members of his party that major amendments would be required. In all, some eight witnesses appeared before the committee. All struck the same theme-that this bill delivered far too much monopolistic authority into the hands of the minister and the Department of Transport and that there was no provision for adequate consultation with the aviation industry. Even more important, there was no provision for appealing the imposition of any regulation that might be detrimental to the industry.
As a result of the hearings and consultation with the members of the government, it was agreed that seven amendments would be advanced, and these were accepted. The amendment we are dealing with now is one that was not accepted at committee stage but it is one about which this party feels very strongly. That is why I have taken this opportunity to introduce it to the House.
I should like now to recap some of the proceedings and review some of the deliberations on the points to which we took exception. One problem was with respect to the provision to
March 13, 1978

tighten up the collection procedure for services rendered to owners and operators of aircraft. It was discovered immediately that the major problem was collection of fees for inflight services-and landing fees and other related services-which was challenged by three foreign carriers which, for many years, have protested the principle that Canada has the right to charge for such services. These inflight service fees are known as the north Atlantic route fee, the Polar route fee, and the telecommunications fee, which are charged by Canada.
The issue is not late payment of accounts, but rather whether Canada has the right to impose such charges in the first place. What has happened is that in this bill the minister has conveniently gathered together the whole aviation industry-the giants, the commercial operators, and the small operators-and with the old sledgehammer approach has taken it upon himself to correct the problem once and for all. The question, as it relates to the three foreign air carriers and non-payment of their accounts, is currently before the Federal Court of Canada. As a matter of fact, a statement of claim was filed on August 1, 1975. The case has not been heard. What is strange is that it is not the Government of Canada that has taken the foreign air carriers to court over non-payment of fees, but the Pan American Airways Incorporated has taken the Government of Canada to court claiming the sum of $4.5 million it has paid under protest, representing charges made for en route facilities and services fees over the Atlantic, and the telecommunications fee.
Pan American, supported by other foreign carriers, contends that these charges were imposed in violation of the International Civil Aviation Association Chicago Convention; it contends that the charges are in violation of our National Transportation Act, and it contends that the charges contravene the principle of equity. The United States does not impose similar charges on Canadian air carriers while in transit over the United States and its territorial seas.
This is the scenario, Mr. Speaker. Since April, 1975, the three U.S. air carriers, namely, Pan American Airways, Trans World and Seaboard have discontinued payment of the en route facilities and services fees and telecommunication fees, and have run up a bill of $5.8 million to January 31, 1978. It is this account that has prompted the government to move with this legislation and, in so doing, to bring in the whole area of aviation rather than simply dealing with the question of the foreign air carriers. The $5.8 million which has accrued since April of 1975 is separate and apart from the $4.5 million that Pan American claims from the Government of Canada and which has been paid under protest since 1968.
In the midst of the turmoil the Department of Transport resorted to this heavy handed tactic, decreeing that all aircraft owners and operators be required to provide a security bond or satisfactory letter of credit to the minister before being allowed to use the facilities and services of the department.
The bill would provide that the Department of Transport could place a lien on such aircraft for non-payment of charges and the aircraft would be subject to seizure. Also, any account due over 60 days would be subject to interest charges.
Aeronautics Act
This was all done because of the confusion on the question of law and the non-payment and refusal to pay huge amounts of money by these three foreign air carriers. It can be classified as nothing less than gross incompetence and bungling of the highest order. The minister and his department have undertaken to lay the blame on the whole industry. It is fair to say general aviation, and particularly those who are owners and operators of light aircraft, have been subjected to this heavy handed tactic of the Ministry of Transport all too often. Even to impose this heavy handed approach on commercial air carriers is fundamentally wrong. That really is not the source of the problem.
I am not sure why the Ministry of Transport wants to take it out on the small operators. This remains a mystery to me because the small aircraft operator in general aviation is usually not the culprit. That point is clearly substantiated by information we received during consideration of this bill in committee.
A review of the accounts receivable for services and facilities which have been provided by the Ministry of Transport, as at March 31, 1977, show the total outstanding amount past due over 60 days at $6.3 million. At that time the total amount which was outstanding with the three U.S. foreign air carriers amounted to $3.6 million, leaving a balance of $2.6 million past due. Of that, Mr. Speaker, there were only 11 private aircraft operators' accounts beyond the 60-day limit. That should hardly necessitate the Ministry of Transport moving in with the sledgehammer tactic and compelling the private operators to provide satisfactory security bonds or letters of credit. I am sure that is not an alarming amount. The bureaucratic red tape which would be involved in trying to administer and police that sort of an undertaking is certainly not worth dealing with the 11 past due accounts. It is really no wonder that legislation of this nature has caused the owners and operators of small aircraft to become rather disturbed and bounce back with some relatively harsh criticism of the government of the day, the minister and the ministry in particular.
I am prompted to read into the record an editorial which appeared in the January-February edition of Canadian Flight. This article was signed by Margaret Carson, who describes herself as a former Liberal supporter. Concerning the trend in the aviation industry as administered by the current Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the current Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), she had this to say:
Our free enterprise system is going down the drain and anyone who is not in one level of government or another, or in organized labour, appears to be considered a "capitalist". General aviation and private aircraft ownership ("capitalist toys") are being discouraged by every means possible, including restrictive legislation, higher taxes, user fees, landing fees and general harassment. Recent statements attributed to government officials on private aircraft ownership include: "What gives you the right to own an airplane?", "Let's legislate hell out of them"; and "We're out to stop the business jet as long as our government-owned airline is flying over the same route with empty seats".
What happened to the "Just Society" and "Participatory Democracy" we were promised by Trudeau during his election campaign? Canada has become a socialist bureaucracy and, as an indication of Trudeau's ideals and objectives, we should not forget his widely publicised statements on a visit to Cuba:

March 13, 1978
Aeronautics Act
I will not read the next few lines as some hon. members across the way will think I am becoming partisan. These are not my words, but the words of a former Liberal supporter. 1 will skip a few lines and you can accuse me, Mr. Speaker, of quoting out of context, but I find it almost embarrassing to quote the two or three lines which are missing. Perhaps those who want to read it for themselves can find it in this particular issue of Canadian Flight dated January-February, 1978. It goes on:
When new legislation affecting aviation is proposed, the various associations are sometimes asked for comments but this now appears to be only a formality and the final result is, in most cases we suspect, predetermined. Commissions are being appointed left and right, at great expense to the taxpayer, to investigate various matters but the results of these also appear to be the same.
Dealing with the present government and its bureaucratic "civil servants" is becoming increasingly difficult and all aviation associations are experiencing the same reaction to their representations. Business and industry generally are also getting similar reactions to their representations.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. Quite frankly, that guest editorial summarizes the opinions and views of many who are involved in the aviation industry.
Through the efforts of the committee we have been able to make improvements to this bill. Some provisions were modified with respect to the question of providing for a security deposit, the ability to place a lien on an aircraft, and the imposition of interest. Concerning aircraft which are classified under the 12,500 pound class range these provisions were removed and their removal was naturally welcomed by the aviation industry, particularly the light aircraft owners and operators. The Air Transport Association of Canada quoted in its winter 1978 Air News that the provision still goes far beyond that which is really necessary. I quote a passage from that particular periodical:
The proposed Clause 2 amendments to the Aeronautics Act would strengthen the power of the Minister of Transport in the area of user charges. The amendments to provide for a security deposit, for liens on aircraft and to require interest on overdue charges (something the government itself doesn't pay) would enhance the monopolistic power of the Minister of Transport and prevent or inhibit sincere negotiations toward the imposition of charges that are reasonable and in the public interest.
The latter remark is a phrase which this government continues to overlook-the question of being reasonable, the imposition of charges which are reasonable and in the public interest. The article continues:
The decision in the Committee to modify the proposed requirement for a bond or letter of credit by deleting reference to aircraft under 12,500 pounds is welcomed. However, the provisions in this clause still go far beyond what is necessary for other Canadian carriers, and because the main concern voiced by the government was to strengthen the Act in order to collect transAtlantic en route charges from three U.S. carriers, it is hoped that this clause will be eliminated or further modified when it is dealt with by the House and Senate.
That summarizes the collective opinion of the Air Transport Association of Canada which is an organization of small commercial as well as the major commercial air carriers of the nation. I can describe this exercise in no other way but to call it "autocratic" and I spell the word "Ottocratic". This symbolizes the attitude of the minister, and with regret I have to say it also reflects the attitude of the Department of Transport. Therefore I believe this amendment which is before the House
at this time is important. What I have outlined here is not a new revelation, it confirms the imperious attitude of the minister and his subordinates.
We should not forget that the minister and the Ministry of Transport tried to impose, by regulation, a 530 per cent increase in user charges in 1976 without prior consultation with the industry. This was eventually altered because of the tremendous amount of opposition that was levelled by members of parliament and members of the aviation community.
We must not forget the mess the minister created when he was trying to set up the airport car rental program. Finally, it is going to be resolved in the courts. This is again as a result of a lack of effective consultation with the parties involved.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext: How many times was he sued?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) asks how many times the minister has been sued. Perhaps when he speaks, he will elaborate on that. I think it has been quite often. As minister in charge of transport, he handles himself in the same way in setting an example with his user pay policy. He expects everyone to pay except himself.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The effect of this inadequate consultation results in regulation and legislation by edict. We also cannot forget or overlook the bureaucratic bungling that occurred in the recent past in the stipulation of the requirement of a certain type of ELT to be installed in all aircraft at a cost well in excess of $3 million. The removal of these ELT's has now been ordered because of certain defects. Is the Ministry of Transport going to come to the aid of these owners and operators who were compelled to install these ELT's? No. Who is going to pay for the mistake? The owners and operators will have to pay for this mistake, in spite of the warnings of the industry.
Here again is a classic example of lack of consultation. It is the edict from on high, the "we know best" paternalistic attitude. When dealing with the subject of user charges, we must not forget the very heavy charges placed upon the users of the air terminal facilities, these very exotic air terminal facilities such as Mirabel which will operate at a $50 million deficit this year.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext: What about Calgary?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Calgary is another one. It is certainly the kind of facility that does not serve the interest of the users. It serves the users of the political fortunes of the Liberal party. Here again is a lack of adequate consultation with the industry with regard to their recommendation in so far as it relates to the function and design of the facilities.
There is unilateral decree. No wonder the Air Transport Association of Canada, when it appeared before the committee

March 13, 1978

with its testimony, stated that the carriers view themselves as captive customers of a monopolistic landlord, as they have little alternative but to use the facilities designed and constructed by Transport Canada, along with services provided at prices imposed. The relations between most sections of the aviation industry and the Ministry of Transport have become so strained that the Canadian Owners and Pilots Association, known as COPA, is considering suing the government, with some justification. On November 24, that organization sent a letter to the Minister of Transport. 1 quote from that letter:
We strenuously object to the proposal that private aircraft be subject to a fee representing a 450 per cent increase in the levy on aviation gasoline sold at DOT airports and what is especially upsetting is Transport Canada's suggestion that such an increase be even considered before making a thorough study of the heavy contribution which general aviation is already making to government revenues. This is akin to saying: "We don't know how much you're paying now but we're going to make sure that you pay much more."
It goes on to point out the impact and the effect of the bungling with regard to the regulation requiring the installation of ELT's which now have to be taken out. In the February 8 edition of Canadian Eastern Aviation News, there is an article headed "COPA May Sue Government". I understand they are well on their way to appointing legal counsel. In fact I believe this has been done. The March edition of Canadian Eastern Aviation News indicates that the COPA board has obtained a firm of lawyers and is very seriously considering taking the government to court over its bungling and the fact that, through its mistakes, it has placed very severe financial impositions upon the aviation industry.
Having said that, it becomes increasingly clear that there is a need for an effective mechanism and adequate appeal provision with regard to the imposition of regulations as it relates to the utilization of terminal facilities and airport user charges for owners and operators of aircraft. The Air Transport Association of Canada said that a very serious defect is now in place in the present review procedures regarding user charges. An adequate appeal provision is not available.
We have come part way in this bill by inserting an amendment which would call for a 90 day consultative period. As I said in committee, this in no way provides for an effective appeal or for the industry to be heard in a formal way. That was a very consistent theme throughout the proceedings. It was raised by every witness who appeared before that committee.
There are various kinds of consultation. If there is not a formal mechanism or structured consultation format established, the Ministry of Transport or the government simply has to ride out the objections of the industry. In the final analysis, after a period of 90 days, the regulation is imposed and becomes law. What I am saying is that there should be a further appeal provision.
Bill C-4 is, in effect, legislation by regulation. To balance the overwhelming powers and to provide a safety valve, this amendment would provide the opportunity for a specific number of members of parliament, 20 to be exact, to refer those regulations which may be seriously objectionable back to the House for a vote. I am not suggesting that all regulations
Aeronautics Act
would automatically go before a committee for a review and back to the House. I refer only to those regulations that may be found highly objectionable.
It is interesting to note that in the committee Mr. McLeish, the head of air transportation, indicated that the best forum for the aviation industry is in fact the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. If that is the best place for them to get their point across, surely it is almost imperative that, with any regulation that may be objectionable, the industry should have the right to have its say or have the opportunity to be heard before that committee. Witnesses could be called and heard, and a report submitted back to the House at which time there would be a limited debate and a vote taken.
This provision is a very fundamental part of our democratic process. We rely far too much on legislation by regulation, government orders in council, and one dollar votes. We have reached the point where we are being governed largely by government edict without ample opportunity for appeal.
We have had a proliferation of government orders in council. In 1976, 3,326 were introduced, and 653 appeared in the Canada Gazette. We have had a proliferation of commissions, task forces, boards and study groups, all making decisions. We have decision making bodies all over the place. However, the decision making body is supposed to be this institution. I am trying, through this amendment, to get some of that decision making power back into the House where it rightfully belongs, in the hands of the elected representatives. In that way it gets the power back to the people, and that is where it belongs.
I have introduced this amendment because I believe it constitutes a necessary check over the excessive unilateral authority which has been exerted all too often by a government which is overly domineering, a government which has penetrated deeper and deeper into our lives every day, in a repressive fashion such as we have not experienced in the last 110 years. This, to my mind, is not democracy; it is government by bureaucratic rule, and it must be brought into line. It must be checked.
As for the aviation community, it will be a long time, given the experience it has had with this administration, before its members forget the high-handed approach the government has taken against them in dealing with their affairs. Mr. Speaker, it is obvious the government has waged an out and out war against general aviation over the last five years. I really hope hon. members on the other side are listening keenly to this. I know the parliamentary secretary is doing so. I have a great deal of admiration for him. He has worked very hard to make this a better bill, and I respect him for that. He certainly has the ear of the industry to a much more positive extent than has the minister. But it seems to me that if the government does not want to accept my amendment we must expect a continuance of the war against general aviation, as in the past.
Acceptance of the amendment would at least constitute a gesture on the part of the government that it intends to sicken

March 13, 1978
Aeronautics Act
off somewhat its campaign against aviation. I ask the government to consider my proposal seriously in the name of the democratic process and of providing the checks and balances needed to govern effectively in the interest of general aviation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to speak after the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski), and in particular to urge the House to consider carefully the excellent speech he has made in support of his amendment. It is one which I myself support very enthusiastically. It seems to me that parliamentarians ought to be more concerned about some of the initiatives we can take in this chamber to keep a tether, as it were, on some of the departmental officials who, in some cases, I think it is clear, would like to carry a sceptre and wear a crown if only the House of Commons were to give them sufficient latitude to enable them to do so.
I believe it became obvious throughout the committee hearings, both this session and last session after hearing the witnesses who appeared, that there was not sufficient consultation with those who are most directly concerned with the effects of this bill and that there was insufficient realization of the practical problems it would create for the industry. The Canadian Owners and Pilots Association representing approximately 11,000 operators in Canada complained three times in the committee about the lack of consultation. Furthermore, once the bureaucrats have drafted a bill, they are not disposed to change their minds about it. This opinion was stated on July 11 last year.
It has become an article of faith among high civil servants that if they can implement regulations to frustrate the obvious intent of parliament, they will do so. In this connection, I recall a memorable speech by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) in which he set out some of the very unjust things which had been done to orphan children who had been denied, by bureaucratic regulation, the benefits which this chamber intended they should enjoy. There are many other examples which could be brought to light with a little research.
A spokesman for COPA stated on July 11, 1977:
We had no advance notice of this bill and certainly no consultation on it. We do not understand why, and we think we should have been advised well ahead of time so that we might have been able to be helpful in the construction of it, because once the bill is drafted and read then it is case-hardened. Somebody, whether it is the minister or the guy who wrote it, or maybe a lot of people, including the government, feels called upon to defend it. And even though they might hear evidence at meetings such as this, which point up discrepancies in it, or problems with it, and so on they find themselves impelled to defend it because they were the ones who wrote it in the first place and they do not want to admit that they goofed.
Unfortunately, that is the truth. It is becoming increasingly evident that this chamber is losing authority every day relative to the ministers and the attempts of some of the bureaucrats, who mean well but who, like the government at times, are seized with an "edifice" complex-and we have seen some of the edifices they are pushing on the Canadian people.
For instance, for some time now the ministry has been occupied with the concept of cabin safety inspection, and no

doubt in future we shall see the installation of yet another layer of inspectors in our aircraft in the absence of consultation with, or support from, the industry itself. In addition to the flight attendants telling us to place our briefcases in the precise spot designated by the ministry, we shall see some other official, full of self importance, giving the benefit of his superior knowledge on the question of precisely how a briefcase should be secured, and all at the expense of the taxpayer. And, no doubt, the air industry will be still further harassed and compelled to fix up the resulting public relations problems with the travelling public simply because somebody or other thought they should foist their grandiose ideas of what should be done, upon the travelling public.
As things are, members of parliament have little or nothing to say about these things and that is why it seems to me the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville is so deserving of support. As I say, it allows the House of Commons to keep a tether on the bureaucrats. In somewhat the same way as under the AIB legislation, action can be taken if members feel that regulations are unnecessarily regressive or impractical in their effect upon aviation. This is surely something which hon. members, regardless of political affiliation, ought to welcome. I am sure they would welcome some way for this chamber to keep, in a general way, the power to oversee and check, if necessary, a particularly inappropriate piece of regulatory work by some civil servant.
To indicate further the lack of respect the government, through this minister, traditionally has for that kind of consultation with industry, it is a matter of record that on June 13 last year the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) tried, with unanimous consent, to make this whole series of committee hearings superfluous. He asked at that time:
-if hon. members would be willing to change the second reading motion, to provide for the bill to be referred to committee of the whole, so that it may proceed through all stages.
What did a former deputy minister of transport and later president of Air Canada think about this? It is very interesting that Mr. John R. Baldwin, who presented a paper to a senior staff seminar of the Canadian Transport Commission, said as follows:
Most important, a difficult psychological change in the attitude of government officials responsible for providing facilities must take place. If it is future government intent to recover all or a major portion of facility costs, then the user who pays requires a larger voice in the decision as to what is provided.
He went on to state there has always been consultation with users, but government has taken a paternalistic attitude, retaining the right of final decisions as to what it will provide and at what costs, and often enough deciding against the views of users. Mirabel is a good example. Certainly there was consultation and some user views were accepted. However, the Mirabel terminal concept was what federal planners wanted, not the users. Similar problems obviously exist in Calgary.
My point is that even though in the course of time the government planners may prove to have been wise, if the user is to pay all or the major part of the costs, his views should be

paramount, and he has the prime right to decide, even if he is wrong. A major change in attitude is necessary to achieve this result.
It is pretty obvious this amendment that has been advanced by my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, will do quite a bit in practical and psychological terms to restrain some of these people, like Mr. McLeish, who no doubt feel they in their wisdom are the ones to pronounce in absolute terms what is best for the Canadian aviation industry. There is no doubt in the world that these people are well qualified, and in some instances no doubt they are right. However, in a democracy such as ours it is very alarming to see the trend being established more and more so that this place legislates, but the real muscle and the real practical effects of what is done do not emanate from the legislation itself but from the regulations the Public Service decides to bring in from time to time.
If there is no opportunity for the industry of the people affected and, indeed, for members of parliament, to have some sort of check or balance on these regulations which are becoming more and more repressive and numerous, then it becomes almost anti-climactic for us to worry too much about the principles involved in aviation or anything else.
I was interested in what the hon. member for Vegreville said about the opportunity to obtain information, and he quoted Mr. McLeish at the committee. I am very pleased that Mr. McLeish, the administrator of the Canadian air transport administration, feels that way toward the committee. I asked him two questions. The first question was about the results of his department's decision to test the DC-10 in California last September which, according to reliable reports, damaged this aircraft which belonged to Air New Zealand to the extent of $500,000, causing all sorts of complications and expenditures. I do not know how many lawsuits might originate from this experiment or who ultimately will have to pay the cost. When I attempted to get some information from him about this 1 was unable to do so.
I also asked him one other simple question about his attitude toward constant pilot monitoring and whether there had been any meaningful consultation with the Canadian Airlines Pilots' Association, and what sort of concept he had in mind. I was not able to get any information. The first question occupied Mr. McLeish's attention to the point that he seemed to get very upset that the matter was brought up at all, and he never did get around to answering the second one about constant pilot monitoring.
It seems to me, without belabouring the point and without repeating some of the things that were so ably put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville, this amendment will allow us to have the best of all possible worlds in so far as parliament is concerned. It will remove the absolute authority, the crown and sceptre complex, if I may use that phrase, which tends to permeate some of the upper echelons, particularly of the department involved. It will enable this place, by the participation of 20 members, to give vent to the wishes, the fears or whatever of the industry or the public, by giving us a tether or
Aeronautics Act
a rein on some of these regulations which otherwise would be passed with absolute impunity.
Through you, sir, I would urge all members of the House to give careful consideration to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville on behalf of our party. It is the type of measure that, in a real way, can further the spirit of co-operation among members of parliament of all parties in a way which existed, for example, in respect of the subcommittee of that special joint committee on penitentiary services. It will allow us, as members of parliament, irrespective of our political party feelings, to join together and advance the position and the authority of the House of Commons, which ultimately is the only forum and institution that ought to be responsible for measures affecting large numbers of the travelling public, or key sectors of our industry.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief regarding this amendment moved by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). On many occasions when bills are put before this House they are dragged out by the opposition, and 1 do not want to follow that example.
I assume that the thought behind this amendment was that it would obviously involve something that would be good for the industry. One of my main concerns is with the fact that any bills the government brings forward are all or partially wrong in so far as the opposition is concerned. The opposition goes on year after year complaining, never putting up anything constructive, just trying to tear down legislation that is good not only for the individual but for the whole country. I do not suggest that every bill this government puts before the House is perfect, but I am certain that the criticism of the opposition is also less than perfect.
One thing opposition members should remember is that when bills are presented to this House there is an opportunity available to all hon. members to contact the people who are concerned. One thing I have learned on this side from some of the more senior members, and I was taught this when I first came down in 1974, is that when bills are presented you should make sure you get a copy to the people involved and get their comments. It is quite obvious to me that it is in this respect members of the opposition are lacking. I know for a fact that when this bill was originally presented I contacted people in Ontario, including the Ontario Flying Farmers and other groups. I gave them an opportunity to speak and react before the bill went to the committee.
During my last three and a half years I have tried to make sure that all people, if they are to be affected by a bill, have an opportunity to speak. I found it to be very successful. In the last three and a half years, whenever I have voiced opposition to a bill, it has been long before members of the opposition have brought their points to the attention not only of the minister concerned but of my colleagues on the back benches and my colleagues in the cabinet. 1 have been able to present to them some of the problems and sometimes the lack of knowledge about the legislation of the people whom the bills

March 13, 1978
Aeronautics Act
propose to help. Obviously this is a problem that crops up from time to time.
I am not too critical of the media, but sometimes you read in the local newspaper, or even a national newspaper, a headline condemning some bill that has been presented in the House. When you read the article and then you look at the bill, you find there is quite a difference between what is said in the newspaper and what the government proposes to do in the bill. I am sure hon. members opposite realize that, when bills are presented, they are not picked out of the hat for somebody's convenience. Bills are presented to help people who are affected in certain areas, such as transport, health and welfare, or any other area under federal government jurisdiction, and to make sure these people know exactly what the problems are so that the government can help them. If this is not what the government is supposed to be doing, then I am afraid both sides of the House are redundant. For the last three and a half years the government has endeavoured to ensure that the people have been heard and that they are helped through legislation.
I was quite surprised when one of the opposition members- I think it was the hon. member for Vegreville-mentioned something about the AIB and said that people have nobody to whom to protest. 1 can assure him that members on this side whose constituents have had problems with AIB have been helped by this side, although people in the outside world might think that backbenchers are just fellows who stand up at the end of a string at vote time. Some people think that, but I think my colleagues around me realize that the work we do for our constituents and the people of Canada consists sometimes in needling the cabinet by bringing to their attention problems in different constituencies when these bills are presented.
I have marked down something that was said by the hon. member for Vegreville and, if I am incorrect, I hope he will correct me. He said that landing fees seem to be imposed on people with smaller aircraft. If he checked the record of the committee meetings, the hon. member would see that when the minister proposed the legislation, landing fees were proposed, not imposed. What is the minister doing? He is laying down a bill before the House for comment, not only from members on this side or in the opposition but from people all over Canada who would be affected by the bill. Is this not what democracy is all about? We lay down a bill before the House, we give an opportunity to debate it and for amendments to be proposed to improve the bill so as to help the people better in areas where such help is needed.
