subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this might seem like a very minor bill for the prestigious House of Commons to be considering, but the amendment proposed to it has changed that. The amendment has put before the House the salient question: does this House have any guts left? The amendment simply asks that in matters concerning the safety of aircraft, as proposed in the amendments to the Aeronautics Act, the House have the power to check the regulations. To make absolutely certain that no member of the House and, I hope, no person who travels on an aircraft or on any helicopter in Canada misunderstands the situation, I will put it in terms that everyone can understand.
I suggest that hon. members look at the amendment to clause 3 on page 2, which I will read slowly, following which I will deliver my remarks on it loud and clear. The clause reads:
3. The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 5.1 thereof, the following section:
"5.2 For the protection of passengers, property and persons on the ground the Governor in Council may make regulations requiring the owners and operators of privately registered aircraft to subscribe for and carry liability insurance, and Fixing the minimum amount of such insurance".
On reading that clause probably everyone feels reassured that parliament is giving to cabinet the power to make regulations, if it wishes, to protect passengers-is it not wonderful because we might be flying in an aircraft some day-property and persons on the ground. That is what it sounds like, but what is the reality? Throwing away the rights of parliament in that type of hypocritical amendment is nothing else but hypocrisy of the highest order, window dressing. Let me give you an example in plain terms.
Everyone of us flies on Air Canada, CPA, Transair, Okanagan Helicopters or any type of aircraft which carry more than the number of pounds mentioned in the legislation. We should read the small print in the bills. If we did, we would find that whenever we travel by Air Canada or CPA, we are insured, whether we know it or not, for $75,000. That has been there in similar type of legislation for years and those airlines are not exempt, but name me one person in all these years that the legislation has been there, put on by so called responsible parliamentarians, that a single person has ever received that insurance. That is what I mean by hypocrisy. Surely after all these years of tragic air crashes across this country, all these years of mothers and children waiting for something that never
March 13, 1978

comes-insurance is supposed to be guaranteed as implied in the legislation-some money should have been paid out.
Because we are parliamentarians, we think we are doing a job when we sit here and let government backbenchers, like the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon), say that the government consults everybody. With whom is the government consulting-morons? Anyone who knows what is going on in this field in this country should be ashamed of himself to see legislation like this going through the Elouse. All this amendment asks is that parliament have some of the power it used to have with regard to air safety, that the regulations put through by the governor in council which are drafted by civil servants are examined by us and that they be put into plain language which even lawyers could not muck up.
What is being done here? Parliament thinks it is passing, in the example I am using, power to the cabinet to make regulations to see to it that people who fly in aircraft are protected, but in fact they are not protected. A passenger is happy when he realizes that there will be insurance in the event of his death and that his family will be independent for life. However, when his estate goes to the insurance company to collect $75,000 or $40,000-whatever the minimum regulations call for-the insurance company says, as insurance companies do year after year, that it will be glad to pay if the estate can prove who caused the accident. How in God's name, when there were 300 passengers on an aircraft and you were sitting in the last seat-and when you are dead-can you prove how the accident happened? Even if you are a survivor, you cannot prove that.
When insurance companies ask for that proof, they are just grinning because they realize that there are a bunch of stupid people in the civil service and in parliament who allow this type of legislation to pass unchanged. This is the type of crap that destroys the credibility of parliament. This is the type of hypocrisy which make us all ashamed when we know about it. All we are asking is that this parliament be allowed to look at the facts. I challenge anyone to name me one person who has ever received this insurance. The insurance companies are ripping off the owners of aircraft who are compelled by this legislation to buy insurance. The insurance companies look at the regulations put through by civil servants, and never pay.
I want to be very specific. Everyone remembers the crash at Toronto several years ago. 1 challenge anyone to name one family of any of those 100 passengers who died that night which has received any insurance. Yet under the regulations passed by the governor in council with the authority of parliament, there had to be insurance.
This is not a matter of an academic discussion of a fine point of law. What we are discussing here is the stupidity of parliamentarians who sit back and say that because they are on the government side they will surrender their souls to the civil service mandarins and put through whatever they ask.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is proposing that since the civil service has failed to write regula-
Aeronautics Act
tions which are clear enough to demand what parliament wants to be done and since the governor in council is so busy and tired that there is not enough time to do this properly, we should bring it to parliament, and parliament should do the extra work to make sure that if we are going to be held responsible for the legislation, we should see the regulations which are being put out under this legislation. This deals with the safety of those who travel by air. Let us remember where the fault lies. It lies right here in parliament where we have said that we are so busy we have no time to deal with regulations or orders in council. Here we have an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville which says that we will take time when the safety of the travelling public is concerned. I think we should pass this amendment so that we can have some of our credibility restored.
Let us get rid of some of the awful shame which hangs over us all by saying that in this field we will take time and see to it that the regulations are examined by the representatives of the people and not by the paid incompetents who write these regulations and who, I confess, are mostly lawyers who should not be in the job.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext: Is this a party vote?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The solution is very simple. Let us put this amendment through. This amendment would give us the power to overrule regulations. Then the civil servant who drafts the regulations and takes them to the governor in council to have them approved will notice what has been said here and will make certain that the regulations are put into clear English which does not allow insurance companies to continue this rip-off.
The insurance companies rip off the owners of Air Canada, Canadian Pacific, Okanagan Helicopters and anyone else who rents out an aircraft which weighs more than the prescribed weight. However, the families of those who die are the real victims of the rip-off. If we want solutions, let us put this through. I suggest that the regulations be put into plain terms such as "It is the desire of parliament that passengers shall be protected" and none of this "may" stuff.
The regulations should require that insurance be paid the minute there is proof of death or injury, and let the insurance companies use the dollars they collect in premiums to find out who is responsible. Let them try to collect their money from the negligent party.
Let us go back to that Toronto Air Canada crash. Obviously the facts show that either the Ministry of Transport, the employees of Air Canada, or both, were responsible for that awful crash. It was not the fault of any passenger. Why, then, should the families of over 100 passengers, innocent of any fault, have to wait all these years for the long and dragged out procedure in two courts? They have to go after Air Canada in one court and the Ministry of Transport in another. One is a Crown department; the other is just an agency of the Crown. This means that the poor fellow who is taking action to find out who is to blame in order to collect his legitimate liability insurance has to have enough money to get actions started in

March 13, 1978
Aeronautics Act
two courts simultaneously. The minimum fee to get started in either of those courts is about $50,000. Over four years it mounts up and mounts up, even if "Rockefeller" is his name.
I speak with obvious feeling when I say that we condemn ourselves by letting this type of slipshod clause get through. Knowing the facts as they have been for the last ten or 20 years, why should we repeat it all over again? I suggest that none of us would be hurt very much by amending this legislation in order to let us examine the regulations to see if we understand them. I am very sure that parliamentarians of all parties would make sure that if we say that insurance protection should be provided to passengers who fly on our aircraft, somebody will pay if there is an accident. However, the present situation in which families of deceased are asked to prove negligence, should not be allowed to continue.
I was talking about an accident which occurred right in the middle of a crowded area, Toronto. What about other accidents all over the country, and accidents in remote places where no one even knows they happen? There is hardly ever any chance of proving which party is negligent. In the case of the recent crash at Cranbrook, they are rushing to find out who was negligent. Before that is resolved there will be a lengthy legal case. The families of the people who died will wait for their insurance for years, and it may never come because the case will never be completely resolved. Indeed, most of the families will not know there was insurance because that fact is not advertised. There is plenty of advertising if the company is supporting the Hamilton Tiger Cats or something like that, but we do not advertise to tell people that insurance is available through order-in-council. It is kept a deep secret. In the event that someone should find out about it, however, it is not likely they will receive anything.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville, which reads in part as follows:
All regulations made pursuant to this section are subject to negative resolution of the House of Commons.
That is very simple, Mr. Speaker. I do not want, any more than anyone else, to overload this House with details of management and administration, but on no subject have we greater reason to ask to take back some of the power turned over to the governor in council, than on this one. They have failed to do their duty through ignorance and maybe through fatigue.
It is not only in the field of air safety that troubles arise, Mr. Speaker. Many members here have heard me speak on the subject I am about to touch upon. I have felt very sorry for ministers of finance in this parliament. Since the days of Walter Harris I have seen them destroyed, one after the other, because they did not know enough about what was wrong with the economic theories that civil servants were following, to change them. And even if they did know, they were not able to change them.

We saw good men knocked down-colleagues of ours, people who were liked-because rightly or wrongly the mandarins in the Department of Finance told them, "This is the way, and this is what you will do." The way has been proven, quantitatively, to be wrong. I have seen these ministers destroyed as human beings through not knowing enough to cope with the charm and persuasion of mandarins who want to cling to power even though they are following the wrong economic road.
Perhaps that is understandable with the involved subject of finance. Safety of air passengers is a subject we all understand, however. People who do not want to think about safety should not fly. On this simple matter that we do understand, we as parliamentarians should make it clear to Canadians that we intend to take this power back and take full responsibility for seeing that regulations are drafted to ensure that what we want will be accomplished. The present regulations regarding the liability insurance that I have used as an example, are not being applied as parliament must have wished when the leglis-lation was passed.
It is not just the question of safety that concerns me, Mr. Speaker. Just a few moments ago a minister of the Crown left the chamber. When he was minister of national health and welfare he was very proud of the fact that he introduced legislation which was passed by all parties in this House calling for a family allowance of $20 per month for every child, regardless of the means of the parent. But when the regulations were published, they did not carry out this promise of parliament. The regulations provided that all children, regardless of the wealth of their parents, should receive $20 per month-except if a child had lost both parents. Apparently, according to the mandarins in the Department of National Health and Welfare, an orphan is no longer a child but is an adult. Under the regulations passed by governor in council this parliament must sit quietly by whilst every orphaned child in this country is barred from receiving the family allowance that we voted.
I took this matter up with the then minister, and I think he was just as shocked as I was. The senior civil servant concerned with this told us, however, that the regulations could not be changed and that if an orphan, whether three years of age, or seven years of age, was paid $20 per month, it would destroy the tax balance of the budget. He maintained it would hurt the country financially by disturbing the balance of ways and means. In parliament we thought we were voting $20 per month for every child under 16 years of age without regard to wealth, but the civil servants decided that orphans were to be excluded. A child who loses one parent would still receive $20 per month, but a child who loses both parents would lose everything, by regulation. And parliament had nothing to say in the matter. When the minister had this brought to his attention-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I have just a sentence or two left. I raised the matter of the family allowance because it is understandable. We all know what an orphan is. In parliament we thought we had done something worth while to help families have children by paying an allowance of $20 per month. We find, however, that by regulations passed without the knowledge of parliament-not brought back to parliament but passed by the governor in council-this is not the case. When we protest, as parliamentarians, we are simply told that the civil service knows what is right and what is wrong.
The question of public safety on aircraft is not that much more difficult to understand. We know that we are not likely to survive the crash of one of these fast aircraft. The chances of any crash being fatal are very high. I think we owe it to everyone who flies in an aircraft in Canada to ensure that if we say, as parliamentarians, that they should be insured, then the family that is supposed to be protected by that insurance receives that protection. I think parliamentarians are smart enough to do that. We may not be able to come up with the latest theories in finance, but in matters such as I have referred to with practical examples, we should be able to ensure protection for our citizens.
I think I have made a solid case for supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Vegreville that on the question of air safety we should give parliament the right to approve or disapprove regulations, and not leave it to the governor in council alone.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that I hesitated for a moment before commencing the few words I am going to deliver. After that powerful and moving speech by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) I thought the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lapointe) would have gone outside to communicate with his minister and then come back to indicate his willingness to accept this reasonable and sensible amendment.
I am looking hard at the parliamentary secretary, and I do not see him nod, so I have to assume he has not been able to get consent. If he had, it would have saved this House a lot of time and we could have dealt with more pressing matters, such as the economy. Unfortunately, no matter where the heart of the parliamentary secretary may be, he is in the position of having to do what he is told. I am sorry hon. members are in a position where they are compelled to occupy positions of parliamentary secretaries. I am sure they would be much happier over on this side conducting the kind of spirited defence for the rights of the public which the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, and the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) have carried out. If the hon. parliamentary secretary is fortunate enough to come back to the House after
Aeronautics Act
the next election, he will have the useful experience of sitting on this side and trying to repair some of the damage he has helped cause.
The hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon) spoke about whether situations are proposed or imposed. It is an issue which concerns us all. For example, are estimates and spending proposals imposed or proposed? What about orders in council or regulations of this kind? Are they proposed or imposed? I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and ask, what about penal institutions? Are they imposed or proposed?
I am sure the hon. member will be able to answer that question. Who will know whether penal institutions are proposed or imposed upon hon. members and upon their constituencies?
We now come to the question of regulations. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and I fought this battle many times. I believe we started off with the Aeronautics Act and the original transportation act which included references to aeronautics. At that time the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), who had not that time been elevated to his present position, was sitting on this side of the House in a greater degree of respectability than he now has. He joined with us at that time in opposing with vigor the legislative proposals of the government, of which he has since become a member. He objected to regulations in the transportation act, to regulations in the act dealing with farm legislation and marketing. He was a tiger when it came to opposing proposals which gave to the government, to the ministers, to the governor in council acting on the advice of their advisers and officials, the power to act, just as this particular legislation will give to the officials of the Department of Transport. The hon. member for Crowfoot is now actively engaged in enforcing regulations of a kind which he once opposed. That will be very interesting reading at some time.
On this side of the House we are concerned. Personally I have been concerned for a long time. We have passed bill after bill in this House, vesting in the government, in the governor in council, in a minister, in an agency, the power act by regulation and order in council. My hon. friend from Vegreville referred to the fact that there were well over 3,000 passed during the past year. It is true that there is some opportunity to examine those through the medium of the statutory instruments committee. Our examinations are only conducted as to form. We do not go into the merits, or into the policy which lies behind the promulgation, the enactment of these orders in council. We have examined a great many of them and we have put in some reports.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of bringing in legislation to amend the Government Organization Act providing for a separate Department of Fisheries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the third time this resolution has been brought before the House. It is and has been as a result of the government re-organization of 1971 when the Department of Fisheries, as it then was, was merged with a number of government agencies. The Environmental Protection agency, the Canadian Wildlife agency and the Meteorological agency are three that come to mind. They were merged to form the new Department of the Environment.
As a result of our opposition to the bill and as a result of some reasonable heads prevailing, there was agreement at the time and the minister became known as the Minister of

March 13, 1978
Fisheries
Fisheries and the Environment. This was at a crucial time in our negotiations with other countries in connection with the Law of the Sea and it ensured that one of the major fishing nations of the world would continue to have a minister of fisheries. However, the department became the Department of the Environment, and the Department of Fisheries became merely the fisheries service of the Department of the Environment. In my opinion that has never been a very satisfactory arrangement, and events have shown that this view is well founded.
All we need do is examine, for example, the budget of the Department of the Environment to find that 50 per cent or more of the department in terms of personnel and budget is made up of fisheries services. This is not to suggest for a moment that environmental questions are not important. Indeed they are, and they should receive the priority they deserve. Today, of course, we have a minister responsible for the environment, a minister of state, who answers to the Minister of the Environment who is now the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc). That is the way we get around the legality of the arrangement because, until the government brings in an amendment to the Government Organization Act, we shall continue this very unsatisfactory arrangement.
To put the matter in historical perspective, this all started back in 1971. Even the Liberal party was never very happy about what was done. The Liberal convention of 1973 passed a resolution as follows:
In view of the immense importance of the fishing industry to Canada, particularly to the coastal provinces, that there be established immediately a department to take charge of this area to be known as the Department of Fisheries and Marine Resources.
That resolution was adopted by the Liberal convention of
1973.	It followed a similar resolution adopted by Conservative candidates from the Atlantic provinces in 1972 and again in
1974.	I might add that Liberal candidates in the Atlantic provinces at a meeting in 1974 adopted a similar resolution.
The only action to flow from all this was a move by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1974 to give us half of what he had promised by appointing a Minister of State for Fisheries. That office was filled by the present Minister of the Environment. The Minister of State for Fisheries had to operate within and under the authority of the Minister of the Environment. All this was happening, unfortunately, at a most critical time in the history of Canada, at a time when the Law of the Sea situation was coming to a head; a consensus was developing that ocean states had the right and the responsibility to manage their offshore resources. As a result of this emerging consensus the 200-mile limit was unilaterally imposed by the government and took effect in January, 1977.
Again, in the fall of last year, the Prime Minister promised, and I quote, "We shall separate the two departments as soon as we have the legislation passed." That was in September of 1977. Now we are at the end of the present session and of this present parliament. It is obvious to me that, notwithstanding the promise made by the Prime Minister in 1977 and during the election campaign of 1974, and the resolution of the

Liberal party in 1973 and again in 1974, repeated at the last convention a few months ago, the government has not seen fit, because it does not consider this to be a matter of priority, to bring legislation before the House amending the Government Organization Act, to redress this serious anomaly by once again creating a fully-fledged Department of Fisheries.
Thus, we shall have to continue during this parliament and beyond the next election and well into the next parliament before obtaining legislative sanction for what is the de facto situation-in my opinion a most unsatisfactory one. It is unsatisfactory because, on the verge of the most exciting time in the history of the fishing industry in Canada, we are beginning to realize, as a result of the action we took a year ago, the tremendous potential for expansion there is in the industry for the benefit of the nation as a whole and particularly of the Atlantic provinces. In the past year, for the first time in our history, the market value of the product exceeded SI billion-it is now $1.2 billion. This makes the industry a very important one, one which merits a fully-fledged department with the undivided attention of a fully-fledged minister.
There is an even more important point which should be made. The Department of Fisheries, unlike any other department in the government, is directly responsible for the lives of thousands of people engaged in the industry. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is in the nearest comparable situation but he has nothing like the responsibility for the lives of human beings as is found within the Department of Fisheries in respect of our fishermen and the ancient industry which they so bravely and energetically pursue. Yet the government does not consider this to be a matter of priority. I say this to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment: my province considers this to be a matter of first priority. It is the number one priority in Newfoundland, it has a very high priority in Nova Scotia and, I suspect, in the minister's own province of New Brunswick.
It is number one priority in my province because we see in the fishing industry an opportunity for self-sufficiency for the first time. The industry presently employs about 20,000 people in the province. There is a tremendous potential for expansion if we manage the resource properly, if we develop new markets and operate under an umbrella of federal-provincial co-operation. The minister must not forget for a single moment that this is an area of shared jurisdiction. The minister may nod his head, and Hansard may not record that nod.
The fact of the matter is, there is a shared jurisdiction here. The fish that swim over the banks of Newfoundland within the 200-mile limit are just as much a resource of the province of Newfoundland as the oil that seeps from the tar sands of Alberta is a resource of the province of Alberta. The minister all too often forgets that very important fact. That is why we are concerned over the propensity of this minister, who is competent and whose heart is in the right place, but whose competence and charity are only exceeded by his arrogance-

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in this debate. My esteem for the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) makes me regret that he does not participate in debates more often. Of course, no blame is attached to him in what I say because I know how busy he is in committees

other than the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, where I think he would agree we are responding to what he described at the beginning of his remarks as exciting times.
The hon. member has accused me of arrogance. This is not the first time, and I regret it, because I hope he does not confuse arrogance and firmness. There are areas of responsibilities which 1 cannot delegate, and in fact, fishermen, through their organizations and their spokesmen, have asked me to be firm in the development of this new opportunity which is presented to us in the 200-mile zone.
i might say to the hon. member that bilateral agreements with other countries have absolutely nothing to do with commodity agreements, and I state this flatly. I might also add that members of the industry and members of provincial governments, either through their deputy ministers or otherwise, were apprised of the bilateral negotiations.
The hon. member gives short shrift to a very important Canadian interest, that is, fish outside the 200-miles which move in and out of the zone and which are so important to the hon. member's province. Obviously international co-operation requires us not to take a dog in the manger attitude with regard to anything in our own zone that is surplus to our needs. It is for that reason that we are willing to look at the allocation of our surplus to those countries that co-operate with us.
Also, the hon. member forgets very quickly that there are stocks which are of interest to countries which have had traditional fishing rights and which, because of the existence of St. Pierre and Miquelon, for example, are obviously of great interest to metropolitan France.
However, I meant to give quite a different tone to my remarks. I agree with the hon. member that a fisheries debate would be very useful because, owing to pressure of other business and at times owing to the overloading of the parliamentary calendar, we have not had a full Fisheries discussion in the House for some time.
I am happy to speak to the motion of the hon. member because it suggests the establishment of a separate department of fisheries. Indeed, the hon. member is echoing an earlier announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of the intention of the government to do just that. The suggestion that a separate fisheries department should be established is not a new one. It entails a reorganization which now makes sense in view of the extension of our jurisdiction to 200 miles which became effective on January 1, 1977. This, and coupled with it a series of bilateral fishery agreements with foreign countries, were important elements in the recovery of the Atlantic fisheries. Of course, other actions taken by the government in the area of fisheries make this step desirable.
[ Translation]
It is true that ground fisheries have experienced serious difficulties from 1974 to 1977. Those difficulties have shown that it was necessary to alter the policy, the operations and the attitudes to save Canadian fisheries and promote their long term productivity. In 1975, the government set forth compre-
March 13, 1978

hensive directions to develop Canadian fisheries. Those directions concerned the development of resources, the conditioning of fish, the marketing of products and social growth. As a result, various recovery programs directly connected with the policy were organized.

Through a substantial subsidy program amounting to some $130 million over four years, the federal government has successfully assisted the Atlantic fishing industry to survive through a very difficult period. In fact the picture at the present time-and I agree with the hon. member that these are exciting times-does inspire real optimism. So far as the Atlantic fisheries are concerned, particularly the groundfish species, the first priority is to build up stocks to something like their former levels of abundance, and it is for that reason that I have resisted a large and too quick expansion. I am confident that, with proper management and conservation, we will see the total allowable catch of Atlantic groundfish available to Canadian fishermen doubled by 1985, compared with the catch in 1976.
At the same time that the government was responding to the crisis in the Atlantic fisheries, it was directing significant attention to the Pacific fisheries. We are looking to a doubling of the production of the Pacific salmon by the 1990's as a result of our salmon enhancement program which is now, as hon. members know, in the first year of the five year phase.
New hatcheries, spawning channels, fishways, lake fertilization and stream improvement facilities will be put in place on the British Columbia mainland and Vancouver Island.
Another bright spot on the Pacific coast is the fast growing and highly lucrative herring roe fishery which will probably bring in $100 million this year.
It is significant that the total market value of Canada's fisheries, as the hon. member has pointed out, has now gone over the $1 billion mark. This means that for the first time in history we have attained and passed this $1 billion figure. This means also increased employment, higher returns to fishermen, and expanding export trade, all of which represent one of the brightest spots in Canada's economic scene, and this was recognized at the recent meeting of first ministers. This change in emphasis from recovery to development will be possible because of new management approaches, including such matters as entry control, stock management units, more efficient use of processing plants, and new marketing emphasis.
Fisheries management is, however, directly dependent on the sound scientific capability that Canada has established. The ocean and aquatic sciences component of our department has been conducting extensive scientific activity associated with the chemical, physical, and biological aspects of the aquatic ecosystem. This strong link between science and fisheries management has been central in past management practices and will be a key in the future.
It is essential to recognize that fisheries has not been neglected under the arrangement that has existed over the past
Fisheries
few years. But our thinking here must be dynamic, and the Prime Minister indicated last September that the time has come to adjust our organizational posture respecting fisheries and to create a separate department. The resolution of this issue is, however, not as simple as one might suspect.
Having decided that the concept of establishing a separate department would now be timely, it was important to look at the respective mandates which should emerge for the fisheries and environment departments and to ensure that the division of responsibilities is consistent with the job to be done. I am glad to say that this task is almost complete and, we hope, with the support that seems so evident from the other side, the necessary amendments to the Government Organization Act can soon be introduced.
The shaping of the new department provides us with the opportunity to review the fisheries needs which exist throughout Canada. Fisheries management is evidently the basic concern of any fisheries department. In its narrowest sense, however, fisheries management is not just a matter of setting quotas and licensing fishermen. It requires science and research, a knowledge of what, where and when to fish and an understanding of the factors which affect stock health and abundance. It involves the preservation of the aquatic entourage, the prevention and control of pollution and a positive enhancement to increase nature's stocks.
In my view, the management and conservation of the living resources of the sea are inseparable from the management of the ocean as the habitat for these resources. We have looked at the responsibilities of other departments and have found that my department has the prime responsibility for the aquatic and ecosystem aspects of the oceans. With the approval of parliament the new department would be known as the department of fisheries and oceans. This title is clear and brings the basic responsibilities sharply into focus for the public. This is important because the public of the Atlantic and Pacific coastal provinces understands the relationship between fisheries and the oceans and expects a strong and clear government response to problems and opportunities in this sector. The discussion by first ministers about fisheries serves as a good indication that provincial governments share the views of the federal government about the importance of this sector.
Perhaps 1 might indicate more specifically the responsibilities that a new department of fisheries and oceans would have. These are: first, management of all Canada's ocean fisheries and some inland fisheries; second, fisheries, oceanographic and freshwater research contributing to the understanding, management and optimum utilization of renewable aquatic resources; third, hydrographic surveying and charting; fourth, administration of small craft harbours; fifth, conduct of environmental impact studies on activities affecting aquatic renewable resources; and sixth, administration of international treaties and agreements covering management of fisheries and other aquatic renewable resources and the quality of the marine environment.

March 13, 1978
Fisheries
The proposed department of fisheries and oceans would provide the focal point in the Government of Canada for the management of Canada's oceans and marine resources. The creation of a separate department demonstrates the priority the government attaches to enhancing the Canadian fishery, to our growing ocean management responsibilities and to the need for a comprehensive approach to fisheries and ocean issues.
I would like to make it very clear that many other departments, such as the Department of National Defence, the Department of Transport, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of the Environment, will retain strong, legitimate concerns and authority with respect to marine matters.
The proposed department of fisheries and oceans would be responsible for providing leadership in the development of our marine policies, posture and capabilities and for acting as the focal point for the exercise of Canada's marine responsibilities, but in a manner that would seek to concert and to co-ordinate rather than to replace the roles and authorities of other departments in marine affairs.
I should like to speak briefly about ocean sciences to reassure those who may not be aware of the commitment of the Canadian government to ocean sciences. Contrary to perceptions held by some people, ocean sciences programs in Canada have been characterized by a very healthy growth in recent years. In the short span of 18 years we now have in Canada six major centres of outstanding excellence in ocean and aquatic sciences, encompassing physical, chemical and biological sciences, whose replacement cost would easily exceed half a billion dollars. Since 1973, despite a period of fiscal restraint, the ocean and aquatic science division of the fisheries and marine service has seen its annual budget grow from $33.7 million to $57 million. Canada's ratio of ocean science expenditure as a percentage of gross national product shows the following comparisons with other advanced maritime nations: in 1974 Canada spent 1.7 times as much as the U.S.A., five times as much as each of the U.K., France and Japan and 5.5 times as much as Australia.
I would be remiss, however, if I did not speak more specifically of some ocean science activities in order to illustrate their importance in the past and their potential for the future. It is noteworthy that the majority of ocean science and survey activities are closely related to the fisheries. Examples of these are relatively large-scale projects on both coasts to study the physical, chemical and biological aspects of the water masses over the continental shelves.
The hydrographic service of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment is now working closely with the Ministry of Transport in developing and providing more precise aids to navigation and positioning systems which contribute to the more effective management of the 200-mile fishing zone and the prevention of destruction of the fisheries resource by transportation accidents. These responsibilities would continue within the new department of fisheries and oceans.

I have spoken at some length on this issue because I believe it is of great interest and importance to Canadians, especially those who rely on the fisheries and oceans for their livelihood. 1 have restricted my comments to the fisheries and marine side of things, as that is my area of responsibility. I might say, however, that while I have spoken of the establishment of a strong department of fisheries and oceans, I support the need for the Department of the Environment and the contribution that it will be required to make to assist in the management of renewable resources and in the protection of the Canadian environment. Additionally, the strong links which have grown up between the various components of the present department must continue to thrive under any new organizational arrangement.
In summary, I am convinced that the time which has been taken to work out a clear mandate for each of the new departments has been time well spent. I hope that we will be able to move quickly and to put in place the legislative and administrative arrangements associated with this major government initiative.
The potential of our fisheries-a clear federal jurisdiction since Confederation-and the potential of our three oceans are quite inseparable. The challenge of the new department of fisheries and oceans and the Government of Canada would be to take full advantage of the opportunities which are open to us.

We are glad of his support in this matter since it is already a declared policy of this government.
I would also like to offer to lend my Oxford dictionary to the hon. member. Apparently he is not aware of what the word "arrogant" means. If he were aware of what it means he would cut out his tongue before he would apply that word to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc).
No doubt the hon. member will recall the swearing in ceremony on September 16 last year, when the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) became the Minister of State (Environment). At a press conference the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated, and I quote:
We will separate the two departments as soon as we can get the legislation passed. In the meantime, Mr. LeBlanc will work with Mr. Marchand: one on the fisheries side, one on the environment side.
This made the government's intentions pretty clear. It was a first step in the process of separation. The next step is for the House to approve the change through a new Government Organization Act. It is good to know that we can anticipate the hon. member's support when such a bill is introduced. I would like to assure the House the details are being diligently worked out by department officials and advisers to the Prime Minister. However, there are other more pressing matters which take precedence over this particular act. Such priority legislation must come first before the House.
With this in mind, I feel sure that the hon. member and his colleagues will be eager to facilitate passage of the pending legislation. Then this matter, in which the hon. member has demonstrated such an interest, can come forward sooner. Of course, while officials are hard at work defining the exact outlines of the new departments, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment will be concentrating his efforts on fisheries matters while the Minister of State (Environment) will be looking after the environment side.
In working out the details of this organizational change we must examine, Mr. Speaker, in practical terms, just what part of the present department's responsibilities should be allocated to each of the new departments. The hon. member has already demonstrated his interest in the operations of the department a number of times. Thus I am sure 1 do not have to explain to him how complex it is, nor explain the number of interrelated
March 13, 1978

functions which have a bearing on both fisheries and environment.
I am sure everyone will agree that work should not be disrupted within the department during the separation of functions. Hon. members can appreciate that disruption at this or at any time could be critical if it affects either the fishing industry or the environment. Another consideration is the maintenance of links that already exist, and even the creation of new links. Two departments with so many common interests should continue to work in harmony and in a spirit of co-operation. In my opinion such a spirit will be even more productive than regulated interdepartmental structures.
In deciding where particular sections or units should go, whether to fisheries or to environment, we have to consider the effect not only on the unit or section but also on each department. More important, the public we serve must not be allowed to suffer from any disruption in the services we offer.
The aim of this exercise is to end up with two stronger departments, each more efficient than the combined department. The capabilities of these two new departments are expected to be greater than those of the former single ministry.
1 must emphasize this is the salient point in splitting the functions. We are seeking more efficiency and it is our belief that a proper division will accomplish just that. Do not expect to see any dilution of the present programs. Indeed, the result will be a distinct sharpening of focus. The mandates for work in both departments already exist; reorganization will allow us to refine and to re-emphasize them.
Within the environment there will have to be a strong emphasis on the watch dog role and there is a need to follow this through. There is a research role in environment, as there is in fisheries. This role may well prove to be one area where sharing and co-operation will be most profitable to both departments.
There are continuing demands for more research on the effects of climate variations; on the threats to human, animal and plant life from countless contaminants; on the capacity of air, water and soil to break these contaminants down into harmless substances; and on economical, practical means to control or eliminate industrial or domestic wastes which are harmful to the environment.
The need for research goes beyond pollution control. New technology needs to be developed to capture and re-use wastes as part of a policy of energy and other resource conservation. Therefore, there must be a stepping up of the research and development role. There will be concrete efforts made to transfer new technology to the provinces and to industry. There is an urgent need to share such new knowledge.

One of the last occasions when I raised this matter of air safety in Canada was on February 15 of this year. Part of my question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was as follows:
I ask what measures the minister's department has taken to see that airlines are adhering to MOT standards and that operational control procedures are up to standard?

That action certainly is important. We are trying to do that with an extremely able group of transport officials, inspectors and agents throughout the country.

As a result, I think it is fair to say that we have a safer aviation system in this country than any country of the world.
Well, I would question that, Mr. Speaker. A matter was brought to my attention recently with regard to flight engineers. I have a document here which states:
At present the airlines are operating with unlicensed personnel in the flight engineer positions, contrary to various aircraft type approvals but acceptable in accordance with air navigation order series VII, No. 2.

New standards are proposed because there is an increase in the number of airplanes in Canada whose type approval or type certificate requires that a flight engineer be included as a member of the flight crew. Hon. members will have noticed the reference to "legal aspects". All I can understand by that phrase is that, in the event of a crash involving loss of life, if it transpired that all the personnel on the plane were not properly licensed it would cost the Canadian taxpayers a tremendous amount of money. The tab would not be picked up by the insurance company but by the Canadian taxpayers. I do not understand how such a situation to which attention was called back in 1976 could go uncorrected.
An MOT regulation referring to flight engineer licenses states:
An applicant shall have reached his 21st birthday and shall have completed the following medical requirements in accordance with medical standards-
It goes on and on; the regulations set out in detail the qualifications these individuals must possess.

If these apparent contraventions are allowed to continue, an accident or incident could result in acute embarrassment to Transport Canada and possibly a substantial loss to the Canadian taxpayer in any resulting court action.
Embarrassment to the minister and to the department! We are talking about air safety and the protection of people's lives, and all this document is interested in is possible embarrassment to the ministry. This matter goes back to a telex which was sent out on May 12, 1977 with regard to examining the operating certificates of various airlines. This communication states that there might be a case for charges under the provision of air navigation order series III, (7) and so on. This document is a directive to safety inspectors across Canada. It came from the inspection branch, aeronautical licensing, and contains the following words: "When carrying out your duties you must fully consider the possibility of embarrassment to the minister and any other potential political implications." Can you imagine such a state of affairs, Mr. Speaker? We are supposed to be talking about air safety. This could only happen under a Liberal government. Politics are being placed above air safety. According to this document, the main concern is not to embarrass Transport Canada. But what about the possible loss of 150 lives? Wouldn't that be an embarrassment, too? The situation to which I am calling attention has existed unchanged for the last two years. That is typical Liberalism.
I have here also another Government of Canada memorandum. It comes from the MOT office in Montreal and is
March 13, 1978

directed to Ottawa. The subject is minimum flight crew- Boeing B-727 aircraft, and the document states:
The Acting Superintendent, Air Carrier Inspection and Certification division, has brought to my attention what appears to be an illegal practice by our national carrier, namely Air Canada.

Article 400 of the Air Regulations, as well as Series VII, No. 2 of the Air Navigation Orders, are both very explicit in that the flight crew of any aircraft must conform to the requirements of the Approved Flight Manual and hold valid licences appropriate to their duties.

I find it somewhat appalling that we are still debating the amendment at this time because I think it would be a simple task for members on the government side to recognize that what we are asking is for a committee to deal with the matter if something extraordinary or irregular takes place with regard to air safety or air traffic. It seems to me that this is a prerogative of parliament. When we view the heavy handed and hard nosed reaction to legislation which is before the country today, it seems to me appropriate for hon. members opposite to let us go forward with the amendment on report stage and then give the bill third reading.
When we see that on the average this government has ten orders in council to consider each day and the cabinet meets but once a week, this means they must consider some 70 orders in council a week. Since we know that they receive 3,500 orders in council a year, it soon becomes apparent that what the minister is trying to do through Bill C-4 is to grasp even more regulatory powers in ministerial hands without giving parliament an opportunity to decide. That kind of action thwarts the whole process of parliamentary democracy. The government asks for more power to be given to the cabinet and less power to the representatives of the people who are elected to voice the will of the people all across this land.
The amendment merely asks that the consultation process take place and that there be legitimate parliamentary review. There is no just cause for not accepting it. I dare members on the opposite side to have the courage to be true parliamentarians. Let them prove that there is harm or some evil associated with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski). If they cannot establish that there is something wrong with the amendment, let them simply allow us to pass it and to proceed to third reading of the bill.
Bill C-4 to amend the Aeronautics Act gives the minister increasing and arbitrary powers to impose the user-pay con-
March 13, 1978

cept and to collect the charges and fees. We all know the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) today believes in the concept according to which he uses and we pay. I think that we should review with great seriousness that kind of system in government in view of the fact that aviation associations across Canada have complained some 20 times before the committee about the lack of consultation. What the amendment before us proposes is that, whenever there are 20 members or more who believe there is something significant which should be brought before the committee, there should be a process for so doing. Until now there has been no effective appeal procedure. Under the bill the minister asks to be licensed to make all regulatory changes relative to aviation without bringing them first before parliament, and then to be allowed to declare to the aviation users that they have no appeal or recourse through a proper appeal channel.
The Minister of Transport did not want witnesses to appear before the committee. He said that this was simply a housekeeping bill and therefore no witnesses should be called. The truth of the matter is that this bill changes the whole user-pay concept. It gives to the minister strong powers to allow him to establish user fees, to decide what they will be, how they will be collected, who will collect them and how often they will be collected. It is not merely a question of the user-pay concept.
Then we come to the great disparities in transport which are one of the catalysts in the disunity in this country. A great disparity occurs under the user-pay concept as it is applied to various modes of transportation. We find that in rail transportation the user pays some 74 per cent of the cost, that in air transport the user pays somewhat less than that, that in truck transport the user pays some 30 per cent and in marine transport some 19 per cent. This means that many regions of the country are gravely disadvantaged under the user-pay concept of the minister.
Furthermore, Bill C-4 locks in a regulatory, ironclad set of agreements whereby the minister can dictate at his own whim the way in which the user-pay concept is applied, which will have a drastic effect on various sectors of the country, so much so that we are finding, in the development of the Alcan pipeline, that a study is now under way to consider the transportation of pipe from Welland, Ontario, up the St. Lawrence Seaway, round the Panama Canal and up the Pacific coast to Alaska simply because it is far cheaper to send it that way than to send it across land. The real reason for that is the user-pay concept-that the user pays 74 per cent of the cost of rail transport as against 19 per cent of the cost of marine transportation. We are of the view that the minister should not have those kinds of powers and prerogatives to impose his will on various regions of the country.
The fact that we cannot haul steel pipe by rail across the country economically causes a loss which weighs heavily on the prairie region. The objective of the user-pay concept is to pay MOT's debts. In essence, what we have found is that the Department of Transport can indulge in all kinds of extravaganzas following which the user-pay concept comes

into effect. What happens is that those who dream grandiose dreams never need worry about the price tag because they can simply tack the price tag on to those who use the system. There is no better example than the imaginative but silly plan for Mirabel airport and the imaginative and silly, if not stupid, plan for Calgary airport. Max Ward of Wardair stated at the opening of the Calgary airport that no one had checked with them, one of the users of the airport, about the user-pay concept. This government goes ahead holus-bolus believing it has the prerogative to dream up heavenly ideas about what an airport should look like, and, irrespective of the price tag, tacks the price on to whoever uses it.
The amendment states that there should be recourse from a government decision: that whenever there are motions from various aviation groups which come to 20 or more members of parliament, they can appeal to Mr. Speaker to set up a body within the committee system which would allow for some kind of appeal procedure. I do not know how the government of the day can sit quietly on its hands listening to the kinds of speeches that have been made in the House about some of the dangers in air traffic today, the lack of controls in air traffic safety and the weaknesses in its own legislation, yet continue stubbornly to refuse to allow a process to be created whereby concerns about various policies affecting the aeronautics industry could be voiced. So long as the user-pay concept is in practice, the government can indulge in extravagance and simply pass on the cost to the users. What we ask for in the amendment is simply a system of checks and balances.
If we are going to have the user pay policy, we ask that there also be a policy of user say. We are asking that there be a system whereby, if the government is going to impose a costing out for those who use aircraft facilities, those who use aircraft facilities have an input. At the present time that is not the case. Aviation groups say that they have complained 26 times to the committee and that they have attempted to be heard by the government. However, the government simply will not give them a hearing.
I would like to speak about the small aircraft industry and the tremendous disincentives the government has imposed upon it. Probably no other nation in the world is more naturally suited to the proliferation of air traffic than this country, unless perhaps it might be the Soviet Union. I can understand why countries like Luxembourg or Belgium might want to restrict the amount of air traffic, but in a country as vast and as sparsely populated as Canada the encouragement of air traffic makes sense. The majority of our resources are located far from inhabited areas. In many cases the only way to reach the resources of this great land is by air.
Few people understand the scope of Canada. It is farther from Yellowknife to the North Pole than it is from Yellowknife to San Francisco. It is a shorter trip from Edmonton to Mexico City than it is from Edmonton to Halifax. We live in a very large land, many of our resources are in places where there are no railways, no docks and no highways. Yet we have

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will not keep the House much longer.
The government is attempting to rule by regulation rather than to allow this parliament to open the channels of communication so that people may use the parliament of Canada as a means by which to appeal to members of this House and therefore to the country. This government acts largely by order in council. Some 3,500 orders in council were passed last year. Not one of them was brought before parliament. By contrast, in Great Britain there were only ten, and every single one was referred to the British parliament. This government has sidestepped parliament.
The whole concept of orders in council was introduced at a time when it was believed that the cabinet needed to act when parliament was in recess for the summer months. In earlier days when orders in council were passed by cabinet they had to be ratified by parliament. Today, legislation ends up on the books by order in council without the citizens of the country having had an opportunity to review it through their members of parliament.
We had an example of this in the past 18 months in Bill C-51, which contained what was called the gun control legislation. All the regulations are subject to change by order in council, as is also the case with Bill C-4, which is now before us. We recall that the metric system, when Celsius replaced Fahrenheit and kilometres replaced miles,-came into being without legislation but through order in Council. In Bill C-4, the government is again attempting to by-pass parliament in the belief that 30 people have the wisdom and the power to make all decisions for the country without recourse or appeal to parliament. People who have real concern about the issues involved would have no opportunity to take them to a forum where they could be heard.
If this government continues on its present path, elections will become a means of rotating parties. If every party were to adopt the same position as the government has, elections would simply be a chance for the people to express their will about who they want their dictator to be. Orders in council and the

avoidance of parliament do not give representative government. It just means that every four years or so there will be a new government to make decisions irrespective of the wishes of the people.
I submit that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville is a reasoned request that the government examine the Aeronautics Act again. He is offering the government a chance to allow people who might in some way be affronted by the regulations to bring their problems to the notice of parliament and its committees through to their duly elected representatives. In this way they will be able to explain their briefs and seek amendments.
What we have at the present time is a government locked in cement, unwilling to hear its constituents and believing that an election is only an opportunity to change one dictator for another. That is not a satisfactory state of affairs for this nation, Mr. Speaker.

My friends to my right mentioned user-pay. I notice that government spokesmen have been backing off that item lately. For the last few years I have been saying there is no mode of transportation in Canada where the user pays, and there never has been-not even pedestrians. Transportation has always been in a deficit position. As long as anybody clings to that concept our transportation systems will continue to discriminate against people because of where they live, and against products or produce because of where they are located.
During the debate on second reading of this bill, and in committee, we were reminded that there are three United States commercial air carriers who owe $5.8 million for user charges on the North Atlantic routes. Initially, I sensed that my colleagues in the official opposition felt sorry for Trans World Air Lines, Pan American Air Lines and Seaboard Air Carriers. In committee, however, we learned that these and all other carriers pay the same type of charges to Iceland, Denmark and Great Britain, but for some reason or other, they do not want to pay Canada. The three airlines are contesting this bill of $5.8 million in the federal court.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I want to wish the Department of Transport well. If these companies do not pay their accounts I hope they are refused landing rights, navigational aids and everything else at Gander and at other airports in the Atlantic provinces. All other airlines have been paying fees to other countries as well as Canada, but these companies have been trying to chisel us. I hope the ministry succeeds in defending our right to collect reasonable charges for services that Canadian taxpayers provide to all international airlines.
Another provision in the bill that we approve in principle is the land zoning regulations. The government's stated objective is to protect airports and airport sites from urban development encroaching upon their boundaries. We agree that the federal aviation authority should have control over the development of land near airports and as well the ownership of it.
We would make one exception, Mr. Speaker. If there was housing development on the land long before an airport was built, it is then a little late in the day for the government to move in and restrict or refuse to properly compensate people who were there long before there was an airport. I agree that when a new airport is built or a present one is enlarged the public aviation authority should own and control that land. No development should be allowed within a one-mile radius of that airport. It should be a green belt, or farmland or perhaps a golf course. But no construction should be allowed. There are examples in Canada where housing developments existed long before an airport was built. I am thinking particularly of the Stanley Park area of Thunder Bay. If there are four houses on eight lots, and someone wants to construct houses on the other four lots, it makes little or no difference whatsoever to the use of that present airport location. That is the kind of exception which should be made in the control the national aviation authority should have over development in and around public airports.

My colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was talking about liability insurance and compensation for passengers as well as for the next of kin of those killed in aircraft accidents. I agree to some extent with his remarks but I do not think he went far enough. Whether an accident or mishap is due to negligence, or to what the legal profession calls an act of God, it seems to me that every aircraft passenger should be insured. This should be a form of no fault insurance. A very small percentage of passengers travelling by air take out aircraft insurance. I suppose we all did the first few times we flew but after that we quit bothering. The fees charged for $50,000, $100,000 or $250,000 worth of insurance are relatively modest. It would seem to me that everyone travelling by air would be willing to pay a reasonable premium that would provide a standard and reasonable amount of compensation in the event of injury or death. I would estimate, and I stand to be corrected if I am very far out, that for somewhere between 50 cents and $1 extra on each airline ticket every passenger could obtain between $100,000 and $250,000 worth of insurance in the event of injury or death due to an airline accident, no matter what the cause.
It seems to me that kind of coverage should be compulsory, particularly for people travelling by commercial aircraft. There should not be any fine print on the back of the ticket. Every person who flies via a commercial airline should know that when they purchase their ticket the extra 50 cents or $1 paid is to cover $100,000 or $200,000 worth of insurance which will be paid by the insurance company to the injured party or to the next of kin in the event of accident. I suspect any insurance company or group of insurance companies, having that kind of business amounting to many millions of dollars a year, would be only too pleased to insure every passenger for $100,000 or $250,000 in the event of injury or death. Normal standard practice should automatically include insurance coverage in the purchase of an airline ticket.
As illustrated by my colleague the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, litigation which goes through the courts six, eight, 10 years after the event should not be paid for by those who were injured or the next of kin of those killed. This litigation can cost tens of thousands of dollars. If the breadwinner dies due to an aircrash it can become necessary to borrow money to live. Surely as a matter of common decency a nominal charge on every airline ticket would cover the premium for a substantial insurance coverage for injury or death due to a mishap.
This is not socialist dogma, even though it might sound like that coming from me. It is a matter of treating one another decently. It is a matter of saying that there is something immoral about trying to make a profit from the misfortunes of others. It is something we should darn well do. In fact that is one regulation which, if the Minister of Transport brings it in tomorrow, I would agree with.
The amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski) is an excellent one. We will support it. We agree with it. However, I want to caution my friends to the right that they should not be under any illusion; whether

there be a majority Liberal government or a majority Conservative government, if this kind of amendment were part of the law it would still be voted down by the majority. If 20 members signed a motion and there was a debate, a majority government would still vote it down. However, it is still a valuable item to have in the legislation. The deputy minister, the airlines experts in the Ministry of Transport, members of the Canadian Transport Commission or even those in consultation with the airline industry would be aware in the course of drawing regulations that unless they do an excellent job with these regulations there will be some kind of a row in parliament. Therefore, these people will be more careful and thorough when drafting regulations. No matter what party is in power, none is perfect. Rome was not built in a day. Of course, the NDP was not building Rome either. There might be the odd miracle situation where some backbenchers of whatever party which had a majority would rebel and vote for a motion signed by 20 members. Some of them might even sign it. But with that caution hanging over the heads of those drafting regulations and those who sit in cabinet and pass them by order in council, I submit they would be more careful and conscious of what those affected by legislation feel about it.
Even with this kind of provision, Mr. Speaker, whether it be a majority or a minority government the party in power still has the ultimate responsibility, as it must under a system of responsible government. Letting parliament decide by vote concerning a motion signed by 20 members is the name of the game in this system of parliamentary government. If the motion passed and the regulations were submitted to the appropriate committee of this House, this would be a good indication that the government of the day had made a severe error in what it had drafted.
There is no doubt that 90 per cent of such motions would not get passed. Some might pass in a minority parliament, but in a majority parliament it would be extremely rare for one to pass. If one did, it would indicate a revolt amongst not only opposition members, but members on the government side as well. That is the value of the amendment.
I am under no illusion, and neither are my friends to my right, that this will be a 100 per cent guarantee of safeguard regarding government regulations. However, it will at least serve as part of the checks and balances in a parliamentary system of government, regardless which party is in power. This amendment provides an avenue of appeal before, during or after the publication of regulations not only by those affected, whether it is zoning or any other regulation, but by any other interested groups that might think the regulation too strong or think it should not be there at all.
If we are going to have regulations on zoning, the methods of determining compensation for those affected are inadequate. In fact, as I understand the bill, compensation is provided only to those using land in a manner which does not conform to the new regulations. It does not provide compensation to anyone else who might be caused injury by airport

construction or operation. Surely that is an inadequate provision. Compensation should be available to those who can justify injury, not only those affected by land required for airport development.
I hope the government will accept this amendment. They know as well as we do that the overwhelming majority of motions would not pass this parliament even though 20 members would sign. In fact, a motion would not pass even if 50 members would sign it. It would be debated for a day or so. Unless there was some kind of severe injury being caused by the government which resulted in a revolt among backbenchers, 90 per cent of the motions would not pass. But the fact that it is there would at least indicate a desire and a willingness by the government to be a lot more conscious of what they put in regulations, when, how and where they consult about regulations, and how, when and where they enforce those regulations.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise tonight to speak on the amendment to Bill C-4 proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski), who has put a lot of work into the communications aspect of the work before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. Even though I am not a member of that committee, I have followed very closely developments in the aviation business in Canada, particularly since I come from a constituency which depends exclusively on aircraft to link us with many of the more remote communities. Some 25 to 30 communities in northern Manitoba alone depend exclusively on aircraft to service them, and if we looked across Canada we would find the same situation in Saskatchewan and in the Northwest Territories.
In speaking to the amendment I should like to point out some of the problems that we experience daily in air transportation and the confusing situation in which the operators find themselves. I will give hon. members a brief history of what has happened and I will use Manitoba as an example. Back in 1966 the then provincial Conservative government under Duff Roblin made a commitment that by 1970, Manitoba's centennial, every community of 100 persons or more would have an emergency airstrip. Prior to that time the 25 to 30 isolated communities in the north were serviced solely by float equipped aircraft in the summertime which would land on lakes adjacent to the communities. In the wintertime ski equipped aircraft landed on lakes. Anyone who has landed on a frozen lake in the wintertime, a lake covered with snow drifts, will know that it is a pretty hazardous operation. Many
(Mr. Ellis.]
times the pilot actually risks his life and those of his passengers as well as risking damage to the aircraft.
Thus the decision was made to build emergency airstrips in the communities so as to enable pilots to service them and to take patients out to hospitals in larger centres, most of the remote communities being equipped only with small nursing stations with perhaps one nurse on staff. The airstrips were located in various communities without too many engineering services. There were fellows like myself who worked for the department in the province of Manitoba. We went out to those places, located suitable communities in need of an airstrip and found a site with free approaches, no obstacles in the way at either end. We always tried to pick an airstrip facing the prevailing winds.
Over a period of five to six years we had airstrips in most communities in northern Manitoba. They were classed only as emergency landing strips, a maximum of 2,000 feet long. This is when the Department of Transport arrived on the scene. Prior to that time these airstrips were classed only as emergency airstrips, but with the aviation industry in the north expanding in leaps and bounds and communities increasing in population, the demand for air travel also increased.
What happened then was that many of the operators in the north switched from ski to wheel operation. In many cases pilots landing on shorter airstrips considered the operation safe enough, but in the view of the Department of Transport the standard was not met in those operations. Their requirements in the north were the same as for Mirabel or the airports at Toronto or Winnipeg. The communities in the north had to have the same standards as were in the rest of the country.
This created havoc in the aviation industry and in the service to the various communities because the type of regulations that were being imposed prior to the involvement of MOT were the concern of the province of Manitoba. A certain set of criteria was arrived at with regard to the placement of terminal buildings, the approaches, the grading required, the width of the landing strip and the clearing and the distance required for a DC-3, a Twin Otter, a single engine Beaver or an Aztec or whatever type of aircraft might be landing in that community. We received specifications from DOT, as it was named then, and we tried to stick to them in the construction of the airstrips.
But lo and behold, after we made some 25 airstrips usable- we had not spent the amount of money which was probably required by DOT because their planning involved engineering studies, engineers on site and so on, and we did not have the funds to put into that type of construction-officials of the Department of Transport made a swing through northern Manitoba in 1975, checked all the airports and decided to close the following airstrips in northern Manitoba: Poplar River, St. Theresa Point, Oxford House, Red Sucker Lake, and Little Grand Rapids. These communities are isolated and the only way to reach them is by aircraft.
Certain specifications were set down which had to be met before these five airstrips could be licensed for certain air carriers, but because of the remoteness of these communities,
